nameStory: The Acadian Flycatcher gets its name from the Acadia region of eastern North America, which includes parts of the Maritime provinces and northern New England. Early naturalists first described this bird from specimens collected in these northeastern forests. The name stuck even though we now know this flycatcher actually prefers more southern woodlands!
description: The Acadian Flycatcher is a small, olive-green songbird about the size of a chickadee that makes its living catching insects on the wing. Like other flycatchers, it perches quietly on branches waiting for prey, then darts out to snatch flies, gnats, and other small insects from the air with an audible snap of its bill. It has a subtle but distinctive appearance with greenish upperparts, pale underparts, and two whitish wing bars. These birds are quite rare in New England, being much more common in the southeastern United States.

idTips.label: Sharp 'peet-sah' call
idTips.description: Listen for a distinctive, explosive two-note call that sounds like 'peet-SAH' with emphasis on the second syllable - much sharper and more emphatic than other small flycatchers

idTips.label: Greenish back and crown
idTips.description: The upperparts have a distinct olive-green wash that's more pronounced than most other Empidonax flycatchers, especially visible in good light

idTips.label: Whitish throat and belly
idTips.description: Clean white or pale yellow throat and belly with minimal streaking, creating good contrast with the darker back

idTips.label: Prominent white eye ring
idTips.description: Bold, complete white ring around the dark eye that stands out against the greenish head - more obvious than on similar species

idTips.label: Two white wing bars
idTips.description: Crisp white bars across the dark wing that flash when the bird moves, though these can be seen on related flycatchers too

idTips.label: Flycatching behavior
idTips.description: Sits motionless on a perch then suddenly darts out to catch insects, often returning to the same or nearby branch with an audible bill snap

habitat: In New England, Acadian Flycatchers prefer mature deciduous and mixed forests with a well-developed canopy, especially areas near streams or wetlands. They favor the middle story of woodlands with beech, maple, and oak trees, typically avoiding both dense understory and completely open areas. Look for them in riverside forests and wooded swamps where the humidity supports abundant insect life.

seasonality.spring: Arrives in late May during migration, when males begin singing their distinctive calls from forest perches. This is the best time to detect them as they're most vocal while establishing territories.
seasonality.summer: Breeding season when they're most likely to be found, though still very rare in New England. They build distinctive hanging cup nests in the fork of horizontal branches.
seasonality.fall: Departs early, usually by late August or early September, making them easy to miss during fall migration. Birds are largely silent during this time.
seasonality.winter: Absent from New England - they migrate to Central and South America for the winter months.

funFact: Despite being called the 'Acadian' Flycatcher, these birds are actually extremely rare in the Acadia region and most of New England - with only 48 recorded observations across the entire region, you're far more likely to see one in a Kentucky forest than a Maine woodland!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other Empidonax flycatchers, especially the Least Flycatcher which is much more common in New England. The Acadian's 'peet-SAH' call is the best way to tell them apart - Least Flycatchers say 'che-BECK' instead. Memory trick: Acadian sounds like 'pizza' while Least sounds like they're saying 'check.'
contextualKnowledge: The name 'Acadian' creates confusion since these birds are actually at the very northern edge of their range in New England and are far more common in southern forests. Early ornithologists named many species from wherever they first encountered them, not necessarily where the birds were most abundant.
compareHints: Among the Empidonax flycatchers, Acadians are the most olive-green above, while Least Flycatchers are grayer and Yellow-bellied Flycatchers are more uniformly yellowish below. The Alder and Willow Flycatchers are browner overall and prefer more open, shrubby habitats rather than mature forest. Voice remains the most reliable way to distinguish between these notoriously similar species.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its Empidonax cousins in New England, the Least Flycatcher is noticeably smaller and more compact than Alder and Willow Flycatchers, with a proportionally larger head and shorter bill.
Among the Empidonax flycatchers, Alder Flycatchers are most easily separated by voice rather than appearance.
Among New England's Empidonax flycatchers, willow flycatchers are most easily confused with alder flycatchers—voice is the key difference.

Among its Empidonax relatives, the yellow-bellied flycatcher is the only one with truly yellow underparts – Least Flycatchers are grayish-white below, while Alder and Willow Flycatchers are whitish with just a hint of yellow.
Compared to other Empidonax flycatchers in New England, the Western Flycatcher has a more distinctly teardrop-shaped eye ring and brighter orange-yellow lower mandible.
Among Empidonax flycatchers, Hammond's shows the most peaked crown and does less tail-flicking than Least Flycatcher.
